title: What All World's Data Means
body:
All world's data is the master inventory of Earth's public data: every record that is lawfully public, openly published, and usable by anyone, organized so a reader can find it, check where it came from, and use it without guessing.

This database is an inventory, not a warehouse of copies. Each record in it points at a domain database that holds the detailed records, and it states the scope of that domain in plain language so the whole of Earth's public data can be surveyed from one place.

The scope rule is strict. Public data means data published for public use by governments, institutions, researchers, and other lawful publishers. Sensitive and identifiable data about private individuals is not public data, and it is excluded from this inventory entirely. Nothing in this database asks for, stores, or points at private personal records.

Readers use this inventory in three steps. First, read the overview to learn what counts as public data and what does not. Second, open the domain record for the subject they need, which names its pointer database. Third, follow that pointer to the detailed records, where each record carries its own provenance, verification date, and license.

title: Domain G: Government and Law
body:
Domain G covers government and law as one of the fifteen public-data domains that together make up all world's data. Its subject matter is the public record of government and law: the laws, registers, statistics, reports, and reference works that lawful publishers have released for public use.

The pointer database for this domain is the Government Agency Directory Database, slug government-agency-directory. That database holds the detailed records for the domain, while this record serves as the inventory entry: it names the domain, states its scope, and gives the reader the exact pointer to follow.

A domain record is complete only when a reader can answer three questions from it: what the domain covers, where the detailed records live, and what is excluded. Anything private, restricted, or identifiable is outside the domain by definition, and no pointer in this inventory leads to such material.

To use this domain, start here for orientation, then move to the Government Agency Directory Database for the full records. New public datasets in this subject belong under this domain, so the inventory grows by adding pointers and domain detail, never by narrowing what counts as public data.

title: Source Family: Data.gov
body:
Data.gov is one of the five source families that feed all world's data. the United States federal open-data catalog, which gathers datasets published by federal agencies in one searchable home catalog.

A source family matters because it tells a reader where a dataset originally came from and how it can be checked. When a record in a domain database cites a source family, the reader can return to the publisher's own catalog and confirm the dataset exists, in the form the publisher released it.

Source families are not themselves the inventory. The inventory organizes by subject domain, and the source families cut across domains: one family may publish datasets that belong in several domains, and one domain may draw on several families. Both views are kept, so a reader can search by subject or by publisher.

When using Data.gov as a source, record the dataset's publisher, its publication date, and its license alongside any fact taken from it. That habit is what keeps an inventory of all world's data honest: every claim remains traceable to a public publisher.
demo_code:
family = "Data.gov"
print("source family:", family)
print("catalog home name recorded:", family)
demo_output:
source family: Data.gov
catalog home name recorded: Data.gov
provenance: Public inventory record; facts from public catalogs and standards.
